In general, examining a single data point, like the price of a good available under near perfect-competition (where one unit of the good in question is nearly identical to any other unit, no matter the supplier) at a single point in time offers no real insight. I think you understand that a low oil price is low relative to prices about about a year ago, and furthermore these prices are denominated in dollars.

I make this initial point only to make the reader consider that there is more to this question than just the price of gas at the pump today.

When the price of certain commodities drops over an extended period of time it may indicate a deceleration in economic activity. If less copper, oil, lumber is being purchased (a decrease in demand) for an extended time, prices will have to drop in order to clear the market of excess supply. You can call this the market clearing price. Prices will continue to drop until people decide that the difference between the price of a good and the value the good can produce is great enough to yield a profit.

In short, a low oil price is a signal to producers that the economy is slowing. If the people who own the means of production are betting on a slow economy, with decreased revenue, they are likely to cut jobs.
